title: Time Periods: From, Until, Since and For
summary: Describe the beginning, end and length of a time period. Distinguish a starting point that continues to the present from the amount of time something lasts.
learningObjectives: Use from ... to or from ... until to show the start and end of a period.
Use until or till for the point when a continuing activity or situation ends.
Use since with a starting point in the past when a situation continues to the present.
Use for with a length of time, and distinguish it from since.

explanation.heading: From ... to: a starting point and an ending point
explanation.body: Use from ... to to show both limits of a period. From ... until is also possible. The limits can be days, dates or clock times.
explanation.example: The gallery is open from Wednesday to Sunday.

explanation.heading: Until or till: an ending point
explanation.body: Until tells us how long a situation continues by giving its endpoint. Till means the same thing and is common in informal English. If a future event follows until, use the present form: until the bus arrives.
explanation.example: Please stay indoors until the storm passes.

explanation.heading: Since: a point in the past up to now
explanation.body: Use since before the time or event when a situation began and still continues now. It commonly occurs with the present perfect: have or has plus a past participle.
explanation.example: My aunt has lived in this town since 2016.

explanation.heading: For: how much time
explanation.body: Use for before a duration such as two hours, five months or a long time. It works with past situations, future plans and situations that continue to the present.
explanation.example: We stayed at the campsite for three nights.

explanation.heading: Ending time versus return time
explanation.body: Until describes the endpoint of an ongoing situation. On specifies the day of an event, such as returning. A return on Sunday is different from remaining away until Sunday.
explanation.example: I will be away until Sunday, and I will return on Sunday.

comparisons.title: Starting point or length of time

left.label: Starting point
left.example: I have known Sam since April.
left.note: Since introduces when the relationship began.

right.label: Duration
right.example: I have known Sam for six months.
right.note: For introduces how long the relationship has lasted.

comparisons.title: Continuing until a day or acting on that day

left.label: End of a period
left.example: The office is closed until Monday.
left.note: The closure continues up to Monday.

right.label: A scheduled day
right.note: On identifies the day when reopening happens.

examples.sentence: The morning market runs from six to eleven.
examples.note: From ... to gives the starting and ending clock times.

examples.sentence: We played board games until midnight.
examples.note: Until marks when the activity ended.

examples.sentence: I've owned this guitar since my eighteenth birthday.
examples.note: Since marks a past starting event that connects to now.

examples.sentence: Our neighbours have lived here for four years.
examples.note: For gives the length of a period continuing up to now.

examples.sentence: I am going to visit my brother for a week.
examples.note: For also describes the planned length of a future visit.

commonMistakes.incorrect: He has worked at the shop for 2023.
commonMistakes.correct: He has worked at the shop since 2023.
commonMistakes.why: A year naming a starting point takes since.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I have studied Spanish since five months.
commonMistakes.correct: I have studied Spanish for five months.
commonMistakes.why: An amount of time takes for, not since.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The post office is open since Monday to Friday.
commonMistakes.correct: The post office is open from Monday to Friday.
commonMistakes.why: Use from ... to for a period with two endpoints.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The children played outside until two hours.
commonMistakes.correct: The children played outside for two hours.
commonMistakes.why: Two hours is a duration; use for.

studyTips: Ask “When did it begin?” for since, and “How long?” for for.
Look for two endpoints: use from with to or until when you name both.
If something continues to a closing time, use until; if it happens on a named day, use on.

exercises.prompt: Choose the preposition: The art club meets ___ 6 pm to 7 pm on Thursdays.
exercises.feedback: From combines with to to introduce a period with two endpoints.

exercises.prompt: Choose the preposition: The library will stay open ___ 9 pm today.
exercises.feedback: Until marks the ending time of a continuing situation.

exercises.prompt: Choose the preposition: Nina has worked here ___ 2021.
exercises.feedback: Since introduces the starting year of a situation continuing now.

exercises.prompt: Choose the preposition: We stayed by the sea ___ four nights last summer.
exercises.feedback: Four nights is a length of time, so use for.

exercises.prompt: Complete with from, to, until, since or for: The service runs ___ Monday to Friday.
acceptedAnswers: from
exercises.feedback: From pairs with to to show the beginning of a named range.

exercises.prompt: Complete with from, to, until, since or for (till is also possible): Please wait here ___ the doctor calls your name.
acceptedAnswers: until
till
exercises.feedback: Until or till introduces the event that ends the waiting.

exercises.prompt: Complete with from, to, until, since or for: I have known Aisha ___ she joined our class.
acceptedAnswers: since
exercises.feedback: Since introduces a past event that began the period continuing up to now.

exercises.prompt: Complete with from, to, until, since or for: The students practised ___ forty minutes.
acceptedAnswers: for
exercises.feedback: A duration such as forty minutes needs for.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I have lived here for 2020.
acceptedAnswers: I have lived here since 2020.
exercises.feedback: Since marks the starting year; for would need a length of time.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We have waited since two hours.
acceptedAnswers: We have waited for two hours.
exercises.feedback: Two hours is a duration, so use for.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The office is open since nine to five.
acceptedAnswers: The office is open from nine to five.
exercises.feedback: From begins a time range that ends with to.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We stayed at the café until two hours.
acceptedAnswers: We stayed at the café for two hours.
exercises.feedback: Use for with a duration such as two hours.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say this complete sentence using from and to: 'The art course runs ___ Monday ___ Thursday.'
acceptedAnswers: The art course runs from Monday to Thursday.
speakingExercises.feedback: From ... to marks the two endpoints of the course schedule.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say this full sentence with the correct preposition: 'Elena has worked here ___ 2021.'
acceptedAnswers: Elena has worked here since 2021.
speakingExercises.feedback: Since connects a starting year with a situation continuing now.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say this full sentence with the correct preposition: 'We stayed in the mountains ___ three days.'
acceptedAnswers: We stayed in the mountains for three days.
speakingExercises.feedback: For introduces a duration, not a starting point.

speakingExercises.prompt: The ticket office opens at eight and closes at noon. Tell a visitor the opening hours in one sentence, beginning 'The ticket office is open ...' and using from ... to.
acceptedAnswers: The ticket office is open from eight to noon.
speakingExercises.feedback: From ... to connects the opening time and closing time.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the verb form after until and say the whole sentence: 'We will wait until the rain will stop.'
acceptedAnswers: We will wait until the rain stops.
speakingExercises.feedback: After until, use the present simple stops for a future event, not will stop.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are at a park and will leave when the rain starts. Tell your friend in one sentence beginning 'I'll stay here ...' and use until.
acceptedAnswers: I'll stay here until the rain starts.
I will stay here until the rain starts.
speakingExercises.feedback: Until the rain starts marks the event that ends your stay.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say these two sentences in order, adding since or for as needed: 'Leo has been here ___ May. Leo has been here ___ five months.'
acceptedAnswers: Leo has been here since May. Leo has been here for five months.
speakingExercises.feedback: Since introduces a starting point (May); for introduces a duration (five months).

speakingExercises.prompt: You cannot join a call at five because you are working until six. Tell a colleague in one sentence beginning 'I can't join the call at five ...' and explain why.
acceptedAnswers: I can't join the call at five because I'm working until six.
I can't join the call at five because I am working until six.
I cannot join the call at five because I'm working until six.
I cannot join the call at five because I am working until six.
speakingExercises.feedback: Until six gives the time when your work ends, explaining why you cannot join at five.

listeningExercises.audioText: The kitchen is closed until Sunday.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which word tells you when the closure ends?
listeningExercises.feedback: Until gives the end of the closure.

listeningExercises.audioText: My grandparents have lived in the same house for thirty years.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which preposition introduces the length of time?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker uses for before thirty years, a duration.

listeningExercises.audioText: The market is open from Tuesday to Saturday.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the word you hear between the starting weekday and the ending weekday.
acceptedAnswers: to
listeningExercises.feedback: To marks the end of the range introduced by from.

listeningExercises.audioText: The small café will stay open until seven this evening, so we can get a late coffee.
choices: The café will start serving breakfast
listeningExercises.feedback: Staying open until seven means the café closes at seven.

listeningExercises.audioText: My uncle has lived in this town since his university days, and he still lives here.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about the uncle?
choices: He moved to the town last week
He plans to move away for university
He has lived there since he was a student
listeningExercises.feedback: Since his university days gives the starting period of a situation continuing now.

listeningExercises.audioText: We visited the mountains for three days last year, but this year we're staying until Sunday.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does Sunday tell us about this year's visit?
choices: How many days the visit lasts
listeningExercises.feedback: Until Sunday identifies the endpoint this year, while for three days describes last year's duration.

listeningExercises.audioText: My neighbour has worked at the hospital since the beginning of April.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single preposition introducing the time when the job began.
acceptedAnswers: since
listeningExercises.feedback: Since marks the starting point of work that continues to the present.

listeningExercises.audioText: They borrowed the camping equipment for two weeks in the summer.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single preposition introducing how long they borrowed the equipment.
acceptedAnswers: for
listeningExercises.feedback: For introduces the duration of the loan: two weeks.
